measureRecords.whatItDoes: Increase Jeffco Public Schools property taxes by $73 million in tax year 2026, collected in 2027. In later years, the levy combined with earlier voter-approved override amounts could raise up to the district’s limit under state law. Money would go into the general fund for education, including staff compensation and career and technical education. A board-appointed citizens’ committee would review spending; annual reports would be posted publicly online. Tax revenue and investment earnings could be collected and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and other legal limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional property taxes for education, public spending reviews and the revenue-limit exception.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this additional property-tax levy or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Increase Jeffco Public Schools property taxes by $60 million in tax year 2026, collected in 2027, and annually afterward. After the first full fiscal year, revenue could increase with inflation measured by the Consumer Price Index. Money would be placed in a dedicated fund used only for school construction, technology and maintenance, including building repairs, heating and ventilation, infrastructure, and security. A board-appointed citizens’ committee would review spending; annual reports would be posted publicly online. A property-tax levy would raise the authorized amounts. Tax revenue and investment earnings could be collected and spent outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits and other legal limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the property taxes for school construction, technology and maintenance, with inflation adjustments, spending reviews and the revenue-limit exception.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this additional property-tax levy or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Allow Blue Mountain Water District to borrow up to $1.2 million through a loan or other multiyear obligation with a state authority. Total repayment could not exceed $2.082 million, and the maximum effective annual interest rate would be 4%. Money would fund water-quality, regulatory-compliance and related system improvements. Repayment would come from water-system fees, charges and other legally available revenue. The measure authorizes no additional taxes.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the borrowing for water-system improvements within the stated debt, repayment and interest limits, without additional tax authority.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a separate 4.5-mill property-tax levy for Golden Gate Fire Protection District, starting with collections in 2027. Its existing operating levy would stay unchanged. The new levy would raise about $137,376 in 2027, with later revenue varying with assessed property values. Revenue would go into a dedicated fleet fund used only to acquire, replace, restore or repair fire apparatus, fleet vehicles and their permanently installed operating equipment. The district could keep and spend the revenue and earnings outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue and spending limits and other legal limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional property-tax levy dedicated to fire vehicles and equipment, with the revenue-limit exception.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this additional levy or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 1% sales tax in Arvada Fire Protection District beginning January 1, 2027. It would raise $23.1 million in the first fiscal year and whatever amounts it produces later. Exemptions include groceries for home consumption, prescription medicines, diapers, school activities and all other categories exempt from state sales taxes. Money would support fire, ambulance, rescue and emergency medical services, including staffing, vehicles, equipment, facilities and responder health programs. The tax would be added to other district taxes. Spending would appear in the annual independent audit online and receive external-auditor and audit-and-finance-committee review. Revenue and earnings would have permanent exceptions from constitutional revenue limits and statutory property-tax limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional sales tax for district emergency services, annual audit reporting and permanent revenue-limit exceptions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this sales tax or its proposed permanent revenue-limit exceptions.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 2.6-mill property-tax levy to the Columbine Knolls Grove Metropolitan Recreation District’s existing levy. It would raise up to $152,000 for collection in 2027 and whatever additional amounts it produces annually afterward. Money would operate, maintain, repair and improve district facilities. Revenue would be exempt from Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits, statutory property-tax limits and other applicable past, present or future legal limits as authorized by voters.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional property-tax levy for district facilities and the exceptions to revenue limits.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this additional property-tax levy or its proposed revenue-limit exceptions.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Authorize up to $6.6 million in recreation-district bonds, with total repayment capped at $13.1 million and an effective annual interest rate no higher than 5.25%. Authorize up to $440,000 in additional property taxes annually for no more than 30 years to repay the bonds; the property-tax rate would have no fixed cap. Projects include aquatic facilities, parks, playgrounds, athletics, accessibility, safety, infrastructure and deferred maintenance. Investment earnings from tax and bond proceeds would be exempt from Colorado’s constitutional revenue limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the bonds, property taxes to repay them and the revenue-limit exception for investment earnings.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds, the additional property taxes or the related revenue-limit exception.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 0.89% sales tax in Evergreen Fire Protection District beginning January 1, 2027. It would raise $5.44 million annually initially and whatever additional amounts it produces later. Money would support fire and emergency services, firefighter and paramedic recruitment, wildfire mitigation, community education, emergency response and capital repairs and improvements. The tax would be in addition to other district taxes and could not replace funding voters already authorized or funding the district is legally entitled to receive.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional sales tax for district emergency services and capital needs, without replacing existing authorized funding.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this additional sales tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Increase Edgewater’s sales tax by 0.5 percentage points starting January 1, 2027. It would raise $1.2 million in 2027 and whatever additional amounts it produces later. Money would be used only to improve accessibility and mobility, including sidewalks, bike lanes, streets and alleys, accessible curbs and crossings, and education and outreach. It could also reduce or remove private owners’ duty to build and repair sidewalks. The city could retain and spend revenue outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue and spending limits and other legal limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the sales-tax increase for accessibility and mobility and the revenue-limit exception.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this sales-tax increase or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Raise Lakewood’s sales and use tax from 3% to 3.5%, starting January 1, 2027. Food covered by the city code, including groceries, would be exempt from the added 0.5%. The tax would raise up to $17.6 million in the first full fiscal year and whatever additional amounts it produces later. Revenue could be used only for public safety, including crime prevention and homelessness response, and traffic safety, including streets, sidewalks, slower vehicle speeds, and pedestrian and bicycle improvements. The city could retain and spend revenue outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue and spending limits and other legal limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional sales and use tax for the listed safety purposes and the revenue-limit exception.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve the increase; keep the city’s existing 3% sales and use tax rate.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Change Lakewood’s charter so a newly elected mayor or city council member begins their term at the first regular meeting after the municipal election results are certified.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve that start date for newly elected mayors and city council members.
measureRecords.noMeans: Leave the charter’s existing term-start rule unchanged.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Replace an obsolete Lakewood charter provision allowing annual property-tax increases of up to 7% without a vote. The new provision would state that the city must comply with the Colorado Constitution and cannot raise property taxes without voter approval.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the replacement charter language requiring voter approval of property-tax increases.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the existing charter language instead of replacing it.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Change Lakewood’s charter deadlines for elections on citizen-initiated ordinances and referendums. A regular or special election would occur between 60 and 150 days after the final decision that the petition has enough valid signatures.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the 60-to-150-day election window for initiatives and referendums.
measureRecords.noMeans: Leave the existing charter election deadlines unchanged.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Increase Wheat Ridge’s sales and use tax by 1 percentage point starting January 1, 2027. It would raise up to $11.7 million in the first full fiscal year and whatever additional amounts it produces later. Money would fund community projects and their operation and maintenance, including streets and infrastructure, bicycle and pedestrian safety, community spaces at Wilmore Davis and Kullerstrand elementary schools, replacement of Anderson Park’s outdoor pool, and police and city-service facilities. The city could retain and spend revenue outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue and spending limits and other legal limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the sales and use tax increase for community investments and the revenue-limit exception.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this sales and use tax increase or its proposed revenue-limit exception.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Change Mountain View’s charter from a council-mayor government to a council-manager government. The town council would appoint a town manager to handle general operations, supervise departments and prepare an annual budget for council approval.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the council-manager form of town government.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the council-mayor form of town government.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Repeal Article VIII of Mountain View’s charter, allowing the town council to create boards and commissions by ordinance instead of requiring a charter amendment approved by voters.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Allow the council to create boards and commissions by ordinance.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep Article VIII and its requirement for voter-approved charter amendments.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Remove an exemption from Morrison’s lodging tax so it applies to lodging facilities of every size, regardless of guest-room count. Starting January 1, 2027, this would raise $125,000 in the first full fiscal year and whatever amounts it produces later. Revenue could fund any lawful town purpose. The town could retain and spend revenue and investment earnings outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue and spending limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve applying the lodging tax to all lodging facilities and the revenue-limit exception.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the existing lodging-tax exemption instead of extending the tax to all facilities.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Increase Morrison’s lodging tax from 6% to 8%, starting January 1, 2027. It would raise $500,000 in the first full fiscal year and whatever amounts it produces later. Revenue could fund any lawful town purpose. The town could retain and spend revenue and investment earnings outside Colorado’s constitutional revenue and spending limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the 8% lodging-tax rate and the revenue-limit exception.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve the increase; keep the existing 6% lodging-tax rate.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Change Morrison’s charter to state that town board members serve staggered four-year terms without term limits.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve staggered four-year board terms without term limits.
measureRecords.noMeans: Leave the existing charter provision for board terms unchanged.
